core: What corporate sustainability is: integrating environmental and social responsibility into business strategy and operations rather than treating it as separate philanthropy

Corporate Social Responsibility (CSR) and its evolution, using Carroll's four-part framework (economic, legal, ethical, philanthropic) and the shift from discretionary giving toward strategic integration
The 'business case' (risk management, cost savings, reputation, talent, access to capital) presented as claims with evidence noted, not as guaranteed outcomes
Materiality and the stakeholder-vs-shareholder framing (Friedman's shareholder primacy vs the stakeholder view; the Business Roundtable's 2019 statement)
Net-zero and science-based targets: what the Science Based Targets initiative (SBTi) is and does
Corporate sustainability reporting at a high level (framework detail handed to ESG Basics)
Greenwashing: the documented gap between environmental claims and action, and its regulation
supporting: The UN Global Compact as the world's largest corporate sustainability initiative and an institutional example
Regulation of green claims: the U.S. FTC Green Guides (16 CFR Part 260) and the EU's move against misleading environmental claims
Empirical evidence on the ESG-financial-performance relationship (Friede, Busch & Bassen 2015 meta-analysis)

The three pillars / dimensions of sustainability (owned by 'Three Dimensions of Sustainability')

claims.claim: Corporate sustainability means integrating environmental and social responsibility into a company's core strategy and day-to-day operations; the UN Global Compact, the world's largest corporate sustainability initiative, asks its 20,000+ participating companies across more than 160 countries to align strategies and operations with universal principles on human rights, labour, environment, and anti-corruption.

Corporate Social Responsibility has been framed since Archie Carroll's 1991 model as four kinds of responsibility a firm owes society - economic (be profitable), legal (obey the law), ethical (do what is right beyond the law), and philanthropic (contribute to the community) - and corporate sustainability has since shifted the emphasis from discretionary philanthropy toward embedding these responsibilities in core business strategy.

The 'business case' for corporate sustainability - lower risk, cost savings, stronger reputation, easier talent attraction, and better access to capital - is a set of claims supported by association rather than a guaranteed return: Friede, Busch & Bassen's 2015 review of about 2,200 empirical studies found that roughly 90% reported a non-negative relationship between ESG performance and corporate financial performance, with a large majority positive, but the authors describe this as an aggregated correlation, not proof that sustainability causes profit in any single firm.

Materiality is the practice of concentrating sustainability effort and disclosure on the issues that are significant to the business and its stakeholders, and the stakeholder-versus-shareholder debate concerns whether a company should serve shareholders primarily or a broader set of stakeholders; in August 2019 the Business Roundtable released a Statement on the Purpose of a Corporation signed by 181 CEOs that moved away from the shareholder-primacy language it had held since 1997 and committed to deliver value to customers, employees, suppliers, communities, and shareholders alike.

The Science Based Targets initiative (SBTi) - founded as a collaboration between CDP, the UN Global Compact, the We Mean Business Coalition, the World Resources Institute, and WWF - defines and validates corporate greenhouse-gas emissions-reduction and net-zero targets against climate science, aiming to keep corporate action consistent with limiting warming to 1.5 degrees C and reaching net zero by 2050, and it published its Corporate Net-Zero Standard in 2021.

Greenwashing - the gap between a company's environmental claims and its actual practices - is a documented problem: a 2020 European Commission study found that 53% of examined green claims in the EU gave vague, misleading, or unfounded information and 40% had no supporting evidence, and that there were 230 sustainability labels and 100 green-energy labels of widely differing reliability.

Deceptive environmental marketing is regulated: in the United States the FTC's Green Guides (16 CFR Part 260) set out the Commission's current views to help marketers avoid environmental claims that are unfair or deceptive under Section 5 of the FTC Act, and the EU adopted the Directive on Empowering Consumers for the Green Transition in 2024 to curb misleading environmental claims.

Corporate sustainability is commonly communicated through sustainability or ESG reports; the specific disclosure frameworks (GRI, SASB, TCFD, and the ISSB standards) and ESG investing are a distinct topic covered under 'ESG Basics'.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Whether a company's primary duty is to shareholders or to a broader set of stakeholders.
positions: Shareholder primacy (associated with Milton Friedman's 1970 argument): management's main responsibility is to increase profits for owners within the rules of the game; social spending beyond that is spending other people's money.

Stakeholder view: firms owe obligations to customers, employees, suppliers, communities, and the environment as well as shareholders, and long-term shareholder value depends on serving them - the position the Business Roundtable endorsed in 2019.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: Presented as a genuine, ongoing debate; the lesson attributes each position and takes no side, and notes the Business Roundtable statement was influential but criticized as aspirational rather than binding.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Whether corporate sustainability reliably improves financial performance.
positions: Business-case view: risk reduction, efficiency, reputation, talent, and cheaper capital make sustainability pay off; meta-analyses show a mostly positive or neutral ESG-performance correlation.
Skeptical view: correlations do not prove causation, results vary by firm, sector, and metric, and some sustainability spending has no measurable financial return.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson presents the business case as evidence-supported claims, cites the Friede et al. correlation honestly as association rather than guaranteed causation, and gives no investment advice.

sourceRecords.title: ESG and financial performance: aggregated evidence from more than 2000 empirical studies
sourceRecords.provider: Journal of Sustainable Finance & Investment; authors Gunnar Friede, Timo Busch, Alexander Bassen
sourceRecords.notes: Verified via WebSearch of the SSRN/journal record. 2015 review combining about 2,200 individual studies; roughly 90% report a non-negative ESG-corporate-financial-performance relation, large majority positive. Used to present the 'business case' as evidence-supported association, explicitly not as guaranteed causation. Copyrighted article; only the headline finding cited.
